title: System Architecture
description: Distributed systems in practice: sagas, events, bounded contexts and backends for frontends.
resumo: Sagas replace a distributed transaction with local steps and compensations — business actions, idempotent.
Kafka: durable, partitioned log; order only within a partition — key by aggregate id; consumers idempotent.
Bounded contexts: one model per context, each owning its data; no shared canonical model library.
BFF: one backend per client type, aggregating and formatting — business rules stay in the services.
System design interviews: requirements, estimates, API, data model, diagram, deep dives, trade-offs — in that order.
Estimate peaks, not averages: ~86,400 s per day; design for 5–10× the average.
Every choice has a cost; name what you accept in exchange, tied to a requirement.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** an order touches three services with their own databases — orders, stock, payments. There is no single ACID transaction to roll everything back when the payment fails.

**Concept:** a saga splits the flow into local transactions and, when a step fails, runs compensations for the steps already done (refund the payment, release the stock). In choreography, each service reacts to events — simple, but the flow is implicit. In orchestration, a coordinator drives the steps — more visible and easier to monitor.

**How it works:** between steps the system is temporarily inconsistent (an order is "pending"), and the user interface must show that honestly.
examples.code:
Orchestrated saga "Place Order":
  1. Orders:   create order (PENDING)
  2. Stock:    reserve items        -- compensation: release the reservation
  3. Payments: charge the card      -- compensation: refund
  4. Orders:   confirm (PAID)

Failure at step 3 -> run the compensation of step 2 -> order CANCELLED
examples.interview_question: When would you apply the Saga pattern?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A compensation that "undoes" the record instead of the effect. Deleting the payment row does not give the customer their money back — the card was charged. A compensation is a business action (a refund), and it must be idempotent, because it can run more than once.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** new services keep needing to react to "order created", and every time the orders service gets a new HTTP call to make.

**Concept:** with a queue (RabbitMQ), each message goes to one consumer and is removed after processing — ideal for distributing work. With Kafka, events stay in a durable, partitioned log; several consumer groups read the same event independently and can replay history. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, so use the aggregate's id as the message key. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

**How it works:** the producer publishes facts ("OrderCreated"); each consumer decides what to do with them, and new consumers need no change to the producer.
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between a queue (RabbitMQ) and an event log (Kafka)?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Publishing without a key (or with a random one). Events of the same order land on different partitions and can be processed out of order — "OrderPaid" before "OrderCreated". Use the order id as the key.

subsections.subtitle: Domain-Driven Design and Bounded Contexts
subsections.description: Drawing the boundaries of services and modules.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** every change touches four services, which always deploy together — the boundaries were drawn in the wrong place.

**Concept:** split by business capability, not by technical layer. A bounded context is a boundary inside which one model and one language are consistent: "Product" in the catalog (description, photos) is not the same as "Product" in stock (quantity, warehouse). Contexts communicate through explicit contracts — APIs or events — and each one owns its data. Wrong boundaries produce the distributed monolith.

**How it works:** listen to the language: when the same word means different things to different teams, there are probably two contexts.
examples.interview_question: How do you define the boundaries between microservices?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: One shared "Product" class for every service (a canonical model in a common library). Every change to it forces every service to update and redeploy together, and each one carries fields it does not use.

subsections.subtitle: API Gateway and BFF
subsections.description: One entry point, and backends shaped for each client.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the mobile app needs a compact response from four services in one call, while the web app wants richer data — and one generic API serves neither well.

**Concept:** the API gateway handles cross-cutting concerns for every client — routing, authentication, rate limiting, TLS. A BFF (Backend for Frontend) is a backend for one type of client: the mobile app gets compact, aggregated responses in one call, the web gets richer data, and each frontend team evolves its own BFF without affecting the others.

**How it works:** a BFF aggregates and shapes data; the business rules stay in the services behind it.
examples.interview_question: What is the advantage of a BFF for mobile and web apps?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Business rules in the BFFs. The discount rule is implemented in the mobile BFF and again in the web BFF, and after a few changes the two apps show different prices. Rules belong in the services; BFFs only aggregate and format.
examples.code:
WRONG: Mobile BFF and Web BFF both calculate the discount
       -> the same cart costs different amounts on each app

RIGHT: the pricing service calculates; both BFFs just display its result

subsections.subtitle: A Method for System Design Interviews
subsections.description: A repeatable structure for open design questions.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** "Design an order system" — 45 minutes, a whiteboard, and the temptation to start drawing Kafka and Kubernetes in the first minute.

**Concept:** interviewers look at how you reason, not at a perfect answer. A structure that works: (1) clarify functional requirements and what is out of scope; (2) non-functional requirements — scale, latency, availability, consistency; (3) rough estimates (traffic, storage); (4) the API; (5) the data model; (6) a high-level diagram; (7) deep dives on the hardest parts; (8) trade-offs, bottlenecks and what you would change at 10× scale.

**How it works:** say your assumptions out loud and check them with the interviewer; a reasoned trade-off beats a buzzword.
examples.code:
1. Requirements      "Place orders, pay, track status. Out of scope: catalog search."
2. Non-functional    "5k orders/min at peak, p99 < 500 ms, never charge twice."
3. Estimates         QPS, storage per year, read/write ratio
4. API               POST /orders, POST /orders/{id}/payment, GET /orders/{id}
5. Data model        orders, order_items, payments (+ outbox)
6. High level        client -> gateway -> order service -> DB; events -> stock, email
7. Deep dive         idempotent payment, stock reservation, failure of the payment provider
8. Trade-offs        sync payment vs async; SQL vs NoSQL; what breaks first at 10x
examples.interview_question: How do you structure your answer to a system design question?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Jumping to technology before the requirements. Proposing Cassandra, Kafka and microservices for a system whose scale and consistency needs nobody has asked about — the interviewer cannot tell whether you can design, only that you know names.
examples.code:
WRONG: minute 1 — "We use microservices with Kafka and Cassandra"

RIGHT: minute 1 — "How many orders per day? Is paying twice acceptable? Who are the users?"
       minute 15 — "Given 5k orders/min and strict payment consistency, PostgreSQL with ..."

subsections.subtitle: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimates
subsections.description: Sizing a system with rough numbers.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** is one database enough? Do you need a cache? Without numbers, every answer is a guess.

**Concept:** rough estimates turn requirements into sizes: requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth. Useful facts: a day has about 86,400 seconds (≈ 10⁵), so 1 million requests a day is about 12 per second on average; plan for peaks of 2–10× the average. Multiply records per day by record size and retention for storage. Order of magnitude is what matters — 10 or 10,000 per second lead to very different designs.

**How it works:** round aggressively and state the assumptions, so the interviewer can follow and correct them.
examples.code:
Assumptions: 2 M orders/day, peak = 5x average, order ≈ 2 KB, kept 5 years

Writes:   2,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 23 orders/s average   -> ~120/s at peak
Reads:    10 status checks per order -> ~1,200 reads/s at peak
Storage:  2 M × 2 KB = 4 GB/day -> ~1.5 TB/year -> ~7 TB in 5 years

Conclusion: one PostgreSQL primary handles the writes; add read replicas or a cache
for status reads; partition the orders table by month.
examples.interview_question: How would you estimate the load and storage of a system in an interview?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Sizing for the daily average. Traffic is not spread evenly — Black Friday, lunchtime, the minute a campaign email goes out — so a system sized for 23 orders/s falls over at the peak. Estimate the peak and design for it.
examples.code:
WRONG: "23 orders per second — a small server is enough"

RIGHT: average 23/s, peak 5-10x -> 120-230/s
       plus headroom for retries and growth -> design for ~500/s

subsections.subtitle: Designing a URL Shortener
subsections.description: A classic interview problem, end to end.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** turn long URLs into short links like `sho.rt/aZ3k9`, redirect fast, and handle far more reads than writes.

**Concept:** requirements: create a short code for a URL, redirect from the code, optional expiry; reads outnumber writes by 100× or more. The code can come from a counter encoded in base62 (`[0-9a-zA-Z]`, 7 characters ≈ 3.5 trillion codes) or a random id with a uniqueness check. Store `code → url` in a key-value table; redirects are a lookup by primary key, cached heavily (Redis, CDN). Use 302 if you want to count every click (browsers do not cache it); 301 lets browsers cache the redirect.

**How it works:** the read path is a cache in front of a key-value lookup; the interesting parts are id generation without collisions and analytics without slowing redirects.
examples.interview_question: How would you design a URL shortener?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Sequential codes from a plain counter, exposed as they are. Anyone can enumerate `aZ3k9`, `aZ3ka`, `aZ3kb` and read every link — including private ones — and competitors can count your volume. Use random ids, or scramble the counter before encoding.
examples.code:
WRONG: code = base62(nextCounter())   -> 1, 2, 3 ... aZ3k9, aZ3ka (guessable)

RIGHT: code = base62(randomLong())     + uniqueness check on insert
       (or a counter passed through a reversible permutation, then base62)

subsections.subtitle: Designing an Order System
subsections.description: Checkout with payments, stock and notifications.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** customers place orders, pay with a card, stock must not be oversold, and nobody must ever be charged twice.

**Concept:** core flow: the order service creates the order (PENDING) and reserves stock; payment is charged with an idempotency key; on success the order becomes PAID and an `OrderPaid` event is published through an outbox; email, invoicing and shipping react to it. If payment fails, a compensation releases the reservation (a saga). Stock uses an atomic decrement (`UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0`) or a reservation table with expiry. Order data is relational and needs transactions: PostgreSQL.

**How it works:** the deep dives an interviewer expects: idempotency on retries, what happens when the payment provider times out, and how events are published reliably.
examples.code:
client ─▶ API gateway ─▶ order service ──▶ PostgreSQL (orders, items, reservations, outbox)
                              │   ▲
                              │   └── payment provider (idempotency key = order id)
                              ▼
                    outbox publisher ─▶ Kafka "orders" ─▶ email, invoicing, shipping

POST /orders                      Idempotency-Key: <uuid>    -> 201 PENDING
POST /orders/{id}/payment         Idempotency-Key: <uuid>    -> 200 PAID | 402 declined
GET  /orders/{id}                                            -> status
examples.interview_question: How would you design a checkout that never oversells stock and never charges twice?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Treating a payment timeout as a failure. The provider may have charged the card; cancelling the order and letting the customer retry charges them twice. On timeout, mark the payment as unknown and confirm its status with the provider (by idempotency key) before deciding.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a design that names the right components but never says what it gives up sounds memorized.

**Concept:** every choice trades something: strong consistency costs availability and latency during failures (CAP/PACELC); synchronous calls are simpler but couple availability, asynchronous events decouple but add eventual consistency; SQL gives transactions and joins, NoSQL gives flexible schemas and horizontal scale; a cache cuts latency but adds staleness; microservices give independent deploys at the cost of operations; more replicas give availability at the cost of money. Name the choice, the reason, and what you accept in exchange.

**How it works:** tie each trade-off to a requirement you gathered at the start ("payments need strong consistency, so...").
examples.code:
Decision                     Chosen               Because                    Accepting
Order + payment storage      PostgreSQL           transactions, joins        vertical write scaling
Notifications                async via Kafka      checkout must not wait     emails seconds late
Order status reads           Redis cache, 30 s    10x more reads than writes status up to 30 s stale
Service split                modular monolith     team of 6                  one deploy unit
examples.interview_question: What trade-offs would you discuss when choosing between synchronous and asynchronous communication?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Presenting a choice as having no downside. "We will cache everything" or "microservices are more scalable" without the cost tells the interviewer you have not operated such a system.
examples.code:
WRONG: "We add a cache, so it's fast."

RIGHT: "A 30-second cache on order status cuts database reads by ~90%.
        Users may see a status up to 30 s old, so after payment we read from the primary."
